strengths: Well-motivated approach leveraging the insight that a single world model trained on diverse multi-task data is more efficient than task-specific dynamics models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across gridworld, LIBERO simulation, and real robot videos (multiple morphologies: Bridge, RT-1, VIOLA, UR5) with appropriate ablations

Thoughtful technical design: raw continuous action vectors validated vs. LLM embeddings, blockwise inference balancing error accumulation and efficiency, interpretable semantic segmentation-based metrics
Honest reporting of limitations including object interaction failures, systematic underestimation of in-distribution and overestimation of out-of-distribution actions
Empirical validation that proposed MSE metrics correlate with human judgment (Figure 6), with clear metrics design based on action-conditioned agreement
Well-written paper with clear presentation, informative visualizations, and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical performance gaps severely limit practical utility: WPE underestimates in-distribution actions by 20-66% (e.g., 0.91→0.69) and overestimates out-of-distribution actions 4-5× (e.g., 0.09→0.50); while relative ranking is preserved, absolute values are far too unreliable for policy selection

Inadequate real-world validation: all 'real robot' evaluations are on training distribution; no evidence policies ranked highly by WPE actually perform well when deployed; real robot policy tests limited to trivial hardcoded actions (single dimension), not learned policies

Fundamental object interaction failures (Figure 9) directly threaten applicability to manipulation tasks; failures (disappearing objects, incorrect physics) suggest learned model lacks necessary physical understanding; hypothesis about data imbalance untested

VLM reward function raises reproducibility concerns: dependence on proprietary GPT-4o API subject to version changes and pricing; significant prompt sensitivity (Appendix B.2); no comparison with alternative reward approaches; 5% false negative rate problematic for safety-critical applications

Very limited policy evaluation scope: only one in-distribution policy tested (OpenVLA); OOD evaluation uses only noise-corrupted versions; no evaluation of genuinely different policy architectures; cannot demonstrate ability to distinguish between different learned policies
Modest metric-performance correlation (MSE: 0.398, LPIPS: 0.415, SSIM: 0.388) suggests metrics explain only ~16-17% of variance, leaving significant unexplained variance in video quality assessment

Blockwise-Autoregressive Diffusion is largely an incremental engineering contribution combining existing techniques (diffusion-forcing + sliding windows); limited novelty over prior work; gridworld action representation study is overly simplistic
Training and evaluation on same data distribution (Open-X Embodiment and LIBERO); domain overlap unclear; no analysis of robustness to truly out-of-distribution scenarios; generalization limited
Inference computational cost and wall-clock time not addressed; no comparison with traditional simulators (MuJoCo) on efficiency; training requires substantial resources (2×A100 for 5 days)

Incomplete reproducibility: promised code/videos have blank URL; reliance on proprietary APIs; limited statistical significance testing with modest run counts (4 runs mentioned); large error bars in some results (±0.22)

strengths: Addresses practical and timely problem in robotics policy evaluation with strong empirical validation (r=0.78 correlation with real-world)
Comprehensive experimental design across multiple robot morphologies, policy families (VLA, video-prediction, diffusion), and 17 distinct tasks
Technical contributions including flexible horizon alignment for efficient inference (2.8× speedup) and clever use of diffusion forcing for variable-horizon rollouts
Preserves policy rankings across model versions, sizes, and training checkpoints, demonstrating consistent relative evaluation
Well-structured paper with clear motivation and good presentation; extensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Correlation r=0.78 leaves ~39% variance unexplained; concerning for an evaluation tool; Table 5 shows substantial per-task discrepancies (e.g., 51-83% performance drops with distractors)
No theoretical analysis of why/when approach works; missing characterization of which dynamics are well-captured vs. poorly-captured; no error accumulation analysis for long-horizon rollouts
Critical flaw: VLM reward validation only on real RT-1 videos, not on generated videos; unanswered whether GPT-4o finds synthetic videos easier/harder; no prompt ablation despite potential impact
Missing baseline comparisons: SIMPLER mentioned but never compared; no comparison with handcrafted simulators or learned reward alternatives; impossible to claim relative effectiveness
Limited generalization: action space normalization via RT-1 percentiles is ad-hoc; unclear generalization to novel morphologies; OOD evaluation uses synthetic edits rather than truly OOD environments
Insufficient statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or per-task correlation distribution; only 10 trials per task; single aggregate correlation metric insufficient
Incomplete ablations: missing studies on action dropout effectiveness, context length, VAE choice; world model validation only on in-distribution action sequences, not truly novel patterns

Heavy dependence on black-box components (GPT-4o, Stable Diffusion VAE) raises reproducibility concerns; no analysis of VLM failure modes on generated videos; acknowledged limitations on 'realistic object interactions' not systematically investigated

strengths: Addresses critical problem of policy evaluation in robotics with a practical, systems-level contribution
Strong empirical validation with r=0.78 correlation between world model and real-world success rates; mean difference only 3.3%
Demonstrates ranking preservation across policy versions, sizes, and training checkpoints (Figures 6-7), suggesting reliable comparative evaluation
Well-motivated design decisions including flexible horizon matching for efficient rollouts (2.8× speedup) and classifier-free guidance for action control
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple robot morphologies, policy families (VLA, video-based, diffusion), and OOD settings (language and image)
Clear presentation with detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, algorithms, implementation details)
Thoughtful engineering of a single unified world model trained on diverse robot data to overcome single-task limitations of prior work
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing components (Diffusion Transformers from Peebles & Xie 2023, Diffusion Forcing from Chen et al. 2024, VLM rewards); main contribution is systems integration rather than fundamental innovation

Per-task analysis reveals substantial gaps that obscure correlation quality: Table 5 shows some tasks with >800% divergence (RT-1-X Cup task: 1→9) and sign reversals (Octo Flip Pot: 6→1), indicating correlation may not generalize uniformly across tasks

Insufficient error source analysis: VLM validation only on RT-1 (81% TP rate = 19% of real successes marked failures); no analysis of VLM accuracy for other policies or ablation separating world model vs. reward errors

Missing critical comparisons: no quantitative comparison to SIMPLER (Li et al. 2024) or WorldEval (Li et al. 2025), despite direct relevance; no comparison to model-free OPE methods or baseline world models

Generalization concerns: limited to 6D end-effector+gripper actions; action space alignment via percentile normalization appears ad-hoc; unclear how method scales to complex action spaces or robots outside training set

Narrow task scope: only tabletop single-arm manipulation with relatively short horizons; no analysis of error accumulation beyond 20-30 steps; generalization to navigation, mobile manipulation, or longer-horizon tasks not demonstrated
Incomplete statistical analysis: small sample size (10 trials), no confidence intervals or significance tests on correlation; no correction for multiple comparisons across 17 tasks

OOD evaluation limited by artificial setup: uses image editing models rather than natural distribution shifts; classification tasks score 'near-chance' (not informative); OOD distraction results show 51-83% performance drops, raising practical deployment concerns
Technical details missing justification: 20-frame context length not ablated; classifier-free guidance weighting unspecified; VLM prompt sensitivity not analyzed
Reproducibility constraints: code/videos not provided; GPT-4o API costs not discussed; requires Open-X Embodiment access; computational costs not specified; would be difficult for others to reproduce
